title: Inflammation and Inflammatory Markers: An Integrative Orthomolecular Systems Medicine Framework for Assessment and Intervention
content: Inflammation is an adaptive biological response whose persistence can reflect interacting metabolic, nutritional, environmental, endocrine, immune, and behavioral conditions. Laboratory markers sample different aspects of this process and require interpretation alongside disease activity, organ function, and clinical outcomes. This narrative review develops an Integrative Orthomolecular Systems Medicine (I-OM) framework for assessment and intervention. It classifies conventional and specialty measurements by biological domain, distinguishes assay availability from analytical validity and clinical utility, and separates biological half-life, first response, normalization, and retesting. ESR and CRP serve as principal examples; immune, intestinal, vascular, and oxidative-damage measurements provide complementary information for selected questions. Human intervention evidence is reviewed for carbohydrate restriction, nutritional ketosis, fasting, dietary quality, orthomolecular nutrients, periodontal care, endocrine treatment, and behavioral support. Results vary by population, comparator, baseline status, exposure, and endpoint. Intermittent ketogenic mechanisms are distinguished from human efficacy, and exposure reduction is separated from unvalidated detoxification claims. Cheng’s Six Principles of Good Medicine, Ten Root Drivers, nutrient principles, and Triple-Principle Intervention Model connect the evidence to cause-oriented assessment and physiological restoration. The proposed integration prioritizes symptoms, function, organ health, safety, affordability, and appropriately selected biomarkers. It provides an evidence-informed perspective and a testable research framework; the incremental clinical benefit of the integrated I-OM program has not been established.
